quizzes.title: NALSA and legal aid structure
quizzes.passage: Legal aid in India is delivered through a network of institutions rather than a single office. At the top of this network sits the National Legal Services Authority, which guides a chain of bodies that reach down to the districts and to the courts. The network exists so that people who cannot easily afford a lawyer are not shut out of the justice system, and its services are meant to be offered on the basis of equal opportunity. The institutions are also expected to spread awareness about legal rights, so that people know when and how to seek help. They organise Lok Adalats and promote the settlement of disputes outside a formal trial. The national body is further expected to monitor how legal aid programmes are working and to develop the rules that govern them. The law that created this network also set out principles on which legal services are to be provided, and these principles guide every level of the structure. Before the present structure was built, the government had already recognised the need to supervise legal aid schemes at the national level, and a dedicated committee was created for that purpose. Each level of the network has its own authority or committee, and together they are meant to make legal help available to people from every background, whatever their income or social position.

questions.q: Article 39A of the Constitution provides for which of the following?
options: Free legal aid to poor and weaker sections
questions.explanation: Article 39A provides for free legal aid to poor and weaker sections of society.

questions.q: Who is the Patron-in-Chief of NALSA at the national level?
questions.explanation: The Chief Justice of India is the Patron-in-Chief of NALSA.

questions.q: Which committee was set up at the national level in 1980 to supervise legal aid programmes?
questions.explanation: CILAS (Committee for Implementing Legal Aid Schemes) was the national committee set up in 1980 to supervise legal aid programmes.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 was enforced on 9 November 1995.
Reason (R): The Act was enacted by Parliament.
Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the fact that Parliament enacted the Act does not explain why it was enforced in 1995.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987   ->   C. Ex-officio chairman is the District Judge
II. High Court Legal Services Committee   ->   D. Constituted under the Act
III. District Legal Services Authority   ->   A. Statutory base for legal aid programmes
IV. National Legal Services Authority   ->   B. Headed by the Chief Justice of the State High Court
questions.explanation: The Act gives the statutory base, the High Court committee is headed by the State High Court Chief Justice, the District Judge chairs the district authority, and NALSA is constituted under the Act.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about NALSA and legal aid:
I. Objectives of legal services institutions include providing compensation to victims of crime.
II. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 was enacted by State Legislatures.
III. A State Legal Services Authority operates at the state level.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement I and statement III are in the booklet, while the Act was enacted by Parliament, not State Legislatures.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the legal aid network:
I. Legal aid institutions operate at taluka or sub-division level.
II. The Supreme Court has its own Legal Services Committee.
III. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 came into force on 1 January 1987.
How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct, while the Act came into force on 9 November 1995, not 1 January 1987.

questions.q: In which year was NALSA founded? (year)
questions.explanation: NALSA was founded in 1995 under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution provides for free legal aid to poor and weaker sections? (article number)
questions.explanation: Article 39A provides for free legal aid to poor and weaker sections.

questions.q: In which year was the Legal Services Authorities Act enacted? (year)
questions.explanation: The Legal Services Authorities Act was enacted in 1987.

questions.q: What is the designation of the Chief Justice of India in NALSA? (two words, hyphenated)
questions.explanation: The Chief Justice of India is the Patron-in-Chief of NALSA.

questions.q: Who is the ex officio chairman of a District Legal Services Authority? (designation)
questions.explanation: The District Judge of the district is its ex officio chairman.

questions.q: Which committee set up at the national level in 1980 is known by this acronym? (acronym)
questions.explanation: CILAS was the national-level committee set up in 1980 to supervise legal aid programmes.

questions.q: On which date did the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 come into force? (day and month)
questions.explanation: The Act came into force on 9 November 1995.

quizzes.title: e-Courts Project and digital tools
quizzes.passage: The e-Courts Project is an effort to bring information and communication technology into courts across India. It was based on a plan prepared for the judiciary to change its working through digital tools, and its work has moved through several phases over more than a decade. The phases have extended computerisation to district and subordinate courts, and the project now includes platforms for managing case records. Digital platforms carry case information from courts at several levels. Other tools serve judges and litigants more directly. Some tools support language needs so that regional languages can take a larger role in court proceedings, while others securely transmit electronic records such as interim orders and bail orders to the authorities concerned. A separate tool supports judges in their work. Courts have also begun to stream some of their hearings live. The project is funded by the central government ministry that deals with law and justice matters. Each of these tools is part of the same effort, and together they show how technology has been brought into different parts of the court system. The phases were carried out one after another over the years, and the tools described here belong to that same programme of work. Each tool has a different purpose, from handling language needs to managing the flow of orders between courts and the authorities that act on them.

questions.q: Which body developed the National Judicial Data Grid?
questions.explanation: The National Judicial Data Grid was developed by the National Informatics Centre.

questions.q: What is the main function of SUPACE?
options: Securely transmitting interim and bail orders to concerned authorities
Collecting relevant facts and laws and making them available to a judge
Translating judgments into regional languages using machine translation
Live-streaming court proceedings on a YouTube channel
questions.explanation: SUPACE collects relevant facts and laws and makes them available to a judge.

questions.q: Which phase of the e-Courts Project was implemented during 2007-2015?
questions.explanation: Phase I of the e-Courts Project was implemented during 2007-2015.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Live streaming of court proceedings is protected as part of the right to access justice.
Reason (R): The Supreme Court held in Swapnil Tripathi v Supreme Court of India (2018) that live streaming is part of the right under Article 21.
Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and the Swapnil Tripathi holding under Article 21 explains why live streaming is protected as access to justice.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. SUVAS   ->   B. Collects relevant facts and laws for judges
II. SUPACE   ->   A. Machine-assisted translation tool trained by AI
III. National Judicial Data Grid   ->   D. ICT enablement of courts
IV. e-Courts Project   ->   C. Online database of orders, judgments and case details
questions.explanation: SUVAS is a translation tool, SUPACE collects facts and laws for judges, the National Judicial Data Grid is an online database, and the e-Courts Project enables courts through ICT.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the e-Courts Project:
I. The Gujarat High Court was the first court to live-stream judicial proceedings on its YouTube channel.
II. The e-Courts Project is funded by the National Informatics Centre.
III. Phase III of the e-Courts Project spans four years from 2023 onwards.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and III are in the booklet, while the National Informatics Centre developed tools but the project is funded by the Department of Justice.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about e-Courts tools and policy:
I. SUVAS is a machine-assisted translation tool trained by Artificial Intelligence.
II. The national policy and action plan on ICT in the Indian judiciary was submitted in 2005.
III. SUPACE is a digital platform for communicating interim and bail orders to authorities.
How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct, while the platform for communicating interim and bail orders is FASTER, not SUPACE.

questions.q: In which year did Phase II of the e-Courts Project start? (year)
questions.explanation: Phase II of the e-Courts Project started in 2015.

questions.q: What does SUVAS stand for? (full expansion)
questions.explanation: SUVAS stands for Supreme Court Vidhik Anuvaad Software.

questions.q: In which year was the National Policy and Action Plan for ICT in the Indian judiciary submitted? (year)
questions.explanation: The national policy and action plan for ICT in the Indian judiciary was submitted in 2005.

questions.q: Which case held that live streaming of proceedings is part of the right to access justice? (first petitioner's surname)
accept: Swapnil Tripathi v Supreme Court of India
Swapnil Tripathi v. Supreme Court of India
questions.explanation: The case Swapnil Tripathi v Supreme Court of India (2018) held live streaming to be part of the right to access justice.

questions.q: Which High Court was the first to live stream judicial proceedings on its YouTube channel? (court name)
questions.explanation: The Gujarat High Court was the first court to live stream judicial proceedings on its YouTube channel.

questions.q: Which organisation developed the National Judicial Data Grid? (acronym)
questions.explanation: The National Judicial Data Grid was developed by the National Informatics Centre (NIC).

questions.q: In which year did the Supreme Court decide the case Swapnil Tripathi v Supreme Court of India? (year)
questions.explanation: The Swapnil Tripathi case was decided in 2018.
